issues.legal_issue: A transfer subject to a statutory bar on recognition remains valid, although the transferee’s rights under the land reform legislation cannot be recognised while the bar applies.
material_facts: The estate sold the grove to the transferee before the land reform legislation took effect, in a transaction valid when made.
The legislation barred recognition of covered transfers for purposes under the Act and deemed the estate to continue to vest in the transferor.
issues.conclusion: The sale was valid and transferred ownership to the transferee; the statutory bar prevented recognition of the transferee’s rights under the Act while it remained in force, but did not make the sale void.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a valid transaction that is barred from recognition from a void transaction. Section 23(1)(b) imposed a bar on recognition and included a deeming provision; unlike sections 24 and 166, it did not declare the transaction void. Under sections 4 and 18, the transfer made the transferee an intermediary who became entitled to bhumidhar rights, subject while the bar applied to the transferor being treated as continuing to hold the rights for purposes of the Act. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.covered_transfer: A transfer was made that fell within the category covered by the statutory recognition bar.
predicates.statutory_bar_on_recognition: The applicable legislation barred recognition of that transfer for purposes under the land reform scheme.

issues.definition: When a covered transfer is subject to a recognition bar, the transfer remains valid, but the transferee’s rights under the scheme are unrecognised while the bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: Removing a bar on recognition prospectively allows the transferee to enforce rights from the removal onward, while a separate retrospective amendment may address specified rights for the earlier period.
material_facts: The 1954 amendment deleted the recognition bar prospectively.
The 1956 amendment made that deletion retrospective from the commencement of the principal Act with regard to compensation and rehabilitation grant.
The transferee’s rights to enforce rights under the Act were initially barred from recognition.
issues.conclusion: The prospective deletion allowed the transferee to enforce rights from the effective date of that deletion. The later retrospective deletion applied to the transferee’s rights to compensation and rehabilitation grant for the earlier period.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1954 prospectively deleted section 23(1)(b), removing the bar from the effective date of the amendment. Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1956 gave that deletion retrospective effect from the commencement of the principal Act specifically for assessment and payment of compensation or rehabilitation grant. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.covered_transfer: A transfer was made that fell within the category covered by the statutory recognition bar.
predicates.prospective_bar_removal: A later legislative change removed the recognition bar only for the future.
predicates.retrospective_adjustment_for_specified_g: A later legislative change gave the removal retrospective effect for specified compensation and grant rights.

issues.definition: For a covered transfer, prospective removal permits enforcement of rights from the removal onward, while a retrospective change can extend the effect to specified grant rights for an earlier period.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee may continue an eviction suit in the transferee’s own right after the transferor withdraws once the bar on recognition of the transferee’s rights has been removed.
material_facts: The transferee and transferor filed an eviction suit after the transferee’s purchase, while the statutory bar prevented recognition of the transferee’s rights, so the transferor joined as a co-plaintiff.
The bar was removed prospectively before the transferor withdrew from the suit.
The trial court’s withdrawal order did not deem the withdrawal effective from the institution of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The transferor’s withdrawal did not affect the suit’s maintainability because, when the withdrawal took place, the transferee could maintain the suit in her own right.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 23(1)(b), 4 and 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act governed recognition of the transferee’s rights and the transferee’s status as bhumidhar. After the prospective deletion of section 23(1)(b) by section 6 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1954, the transferee could maintain the suit in her own right. The Court rejected the contention that withdrawal related back to the suit’s institution because no such order had been made. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: eviction_suit and transferee_rights_bar_removed and transferor_withdrew_after_removal and no_order_made_withdrawal_retroactive

predicates.eviction_suit: The proceeding was a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.transferee_rights_bar_removed: The bar preventing recognition of the transferee’s rights had been removed.
predicates.transferor_withdrew_after_removal: The transferor withdrew as a plaintiff after the recognition bar had been removed.
predicates.no_order_made_withdrawal_retroactive: The court ordering withdrawal did not make it effective from the institution of the suit.

issues.definition: In an eviction suit, a transferee may continue alone when the transferor withdraws after the recognition bar is removed and the withdrawal was not ordered to take effect from the suit’s institution.
